## Introduction

In class, we used the Claude extension in VS Code Server
(see [this week's second lecture](../week08/w8b_claude.qmd)).
Claude is great for chat and agent-style help,
but it does not give you **inline suggestions**:
"ghost text" code completions that appear as you type.
Additionally, you can only continue to use Claude after this course if your
PI supports an Ohio State Generative AI account, or if you get a personal account^[
  Note: If you get a personal account, you will be responsible for any costs
  associated with its use and it will not be OSU-approved].

This page focuses on GitHub Copilot, which in VS Code is a built-in feature.
You will learn how to:

- Get free extended access to GitHub Copilot as a student
- Sign in to GitHub Copilot and enable its inline suggestions in VS Code
- Use GitHub Copilot's inline suggestions and chat to help you with coding tasks

**Unlike the Claude setup we use in class, GitHub Copilot is not an OSU-approved tool.**
This is true even though GitHub Copilot is closely related to Microsoft Copilot^[
GitHub and VS Code are both Microsoft products.
Google Gemini also has a VS Code extension with similar functionality,
but when I logged in with OSU credentials, I was informed that this is not available to us.
].
So, whenever you use GitHub Copilot, you must be aware of the data privacy implications
outlined in [this week's first lecture](../week08/w8a_genAI.qmd).

## Setting up

### About access to GitHub Copilot

Anyone with a GitHub account is automatically enrolled in the "**Copilot Free**" plan,
which provides quite limited access to Copilot's features, but at least you can try it out.
As students and teachers/faculty, we can get additional free access after applying for it.
While teachers can get access to the "**Copilot Pro**" plan,
which can also be bought by individuals for $10/month,
students get access to the more limited "**Copilot Student**" plan.

GitHub is increasingly vague about the limits of especially the free and student plans,
but here is an approximate summary (where an "AI Credit" is roughly a single chat request):

| Plan        | Free for whom    | How to get it                | Code completions | "AI Credits" |
| ----------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------- |
| **Free**    | Everyone         | Automatically                | 2,000 per month  | ~50           |
| **Student** | Students         | Apply for education benefits | Unlimited        | 200           |
| **Pro**     | Teachers/Faculty | Apply for education benefits | Unlimited        | 1,500         |

: {.striped .hover}

## GitHub Copilot inline suggestions

Let's start by creating a dir for the work you'll do following along with this page,
navigating there, and creating and opening a Markdown file:

```bash
# You should be in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER
mkdir -p week08/copilot
cd week08/copilot
touch copilot.md
```

In the editor, paste the following into the `copilot.md` document:

````{.markdown .file filename="copilot.md"}
```{{bash}}
# GTF file:
GTF=../../garrigos/ref/annot.gtf
```

````

Next, turn on inline suggestions specifically for Markdown:

TODO

When you go to a new line within the code block and wait a second,
you should see a suggestion "in ghost text" (light gray text) appear.
To accept the suggestion, press <kbd>Tab</kbd>.

But instead of letting GitHub Copilot go off on its own to randomly suggest
ways to interrogate this file,
let's give it a prompt by typing a comment line first:

```bash
# Count the number of lines in the GTF file
```

Press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to go to a new line, and again wait for a second for the
suggestion to appear.
Accept it with <kbd>Tab</kbd> and run the code:
does it seem to have given a correct suggestion?

### Example prompts for the GTF file

```bash
# Count the number of lines in the GTF file, excluding the header

# Count the number of gene features in the GTF file

# Print a frequency table of all feature types in the GTF file

# Count the number of genes on the + versus the - strand

# How many genes have a description?
```

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Multiple suggestions may be available

You can hover over suggestions to see alternative suggestions,
if they are available --- see the top-right of this screenshot:

![](/img/copilot-hover-suggestions.png){fig-align="center" width="85%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot showing alternative Copilot suggestions revealed by hovering over the ghost text, with navigation arrows in the top right." .lightbox}

::: legend2

and you can click the arrows to navigate between them.
:::

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Iterating questions and inline chat _(Click to expand)_
When you are not happy with Copilot's suggestion,
you can delete the answer, modify your prompt line, and press <kbd>Enter</kbd> again.
However, if you want to explicitly request a change to the current suggestion,
you can also use the inline chat functionality by selecting the code and pressing
<kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> (Mac) / <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> (Windows).
(Claude doesn't have inline chat:
there, you would select the lines and ask about them in the side bar.)

For example, I didn't get a good answer to the last prompt above:

![](/img/copilot-inline-1.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of an inline Copilot suggestion in ghost text that does not correctly answer the prompt." .lightbox}

So I pressed the <kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> and reported the failure:

![](/img/copilot-inline-2.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the Copilot inline chat box, with a message reporting that the previous suggestion was incorrect." .lightbox}

Copilot then came up with a fix, which I could accept:

![](/img/copilot-inline-3.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot's inline chat proposing a fixed code suggestion." .lightbox}

Running the modified line did give the correct answer:

![](/img/copilot-inline-4.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the terminal, showing the corrected code now producing the correct output." .lightbox}
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## GitHub Copilot Chat

### The chat sidebar and chat options

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}

Just like for Claude, the chat lives in the secondary side bar.
Open it by clicking the icon shown on the right,
and then make sure that the "`CHAT`" tab is selected.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Other ways to open the chat sidebar _(Click to expand)_

- You can use the keyboard shortcut
  <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>⌘/Alt</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd>
  to directly open the `"CHAT`" tab in the secondary sidebar.
- You can click "sparkling chat box" icon in the top bar,
  shown in this screenshot:

![](/img/copilot-open-sidebar-sparkle-icon.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the VS Code top bar, with the icon to open the GitHub Copilot Chat sidebar highlighted on the far left." .lightbox}

:::

:::
::: {.column width="35%"}

![](/img/vscode-claude-secondary-side-bar-annot1.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the VS Code side bar with a CLAUDE CODE tab." .lightbox}

:::
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

The chat sidebar should open on the right side of your VS Code window,
and look something like the screenshot on the right.

#### File context

Just like Claude, Copilot can search and read files in your workspace
(the folder open in VS Code) by itself.
And like in Claude, you can point it to specific files:

- **The file that's active in the editor** is _suggested_ as context.
  You should see `copilot.md` at the top of the chat box
  (TODO - REPLACE SCREENSHOT).
  Unlike in Claude, it is not added automatically:
  click the `+` button next to the file name to add it.
- **Other files** can be added with the attachment icon,
  or by typing `#` followed by part of a file name
  (in Claude, you used `@` for this).
- **Lines of code** that you select in the editor are added as context,
  just like in Claude.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

![](/img/vscode-copilot-initial-look.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the VS Code side bar showing the GitHub Copilot interface." .lightbox}

:::
:::

::: callout-tip
#### File/context tips
As with Claude, it's often better to point Copilot to the relevant files explicitly,
rather than letting it search for them.
Copilot also pays extra attention to the files you have open in the editor,
so when asking questions,
consider opening relevant files and closing irrelevant ones.
:::

#### Modes

The dropdown menu in the bottom-left corner of the chat box allows you to
select different **chat modes**[^modes]:

[^modes]: VS Code calls these "agents" rather than modes,
  but "mode" is clearer here, since all three are run by the same AI.

1. **Ask** --- Copilot answers questions,
   but doesn't change any files or run any commands.
   Claude doesn't have a mode like this,
   which is why we recommended using a browser-based chat for general questions.
2. **Agent** --- Copilot can search your files, create and edit files,
   and run commands.
   This is the mode that is most similar to how we used Claude in class.
3. **Plan** --- Just like Claude's Plan mode,
   Copilot looks around your files without changing them,
   and writes a plan for a bigger task.
   Once you're happy with the plan, Copilot switches to Agent mode to carry it out.

#### Models

Unlike Claude, which only uses Claude models,
GitHub Copilot lets you choose between completely different LLMs
(GPT, Claude, Gemini, and others).
On the free and student plans, however,
you can only use whatever model Copilot automatically picks for each request ---
there's no model dropdown to choose from.
(Pro and paid Copilot plans do let you manually pick a specific model.)

### An example in "Ask" mode

Ask mode is useful when you want an answer based on general knowledge
rather than on your files,
for example to understand a concept, or why a command behaves the way it does.
For such questions, an agent may go off and search through your files,
or suggest running commands to test things.
That is slower and fills up the context window with things that aren't needed.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Ask mode can still _read_ your files when it thinks that is useful.
But if your question is self-contained, it will typically just answer it.
:::

Select "Ask" mode and type the following prompt:

> In a Bash script with `set -euo pipefail`, why could the line
> `zcat sample.fastq.gz | head -n 8` make my script stop with an error,
> even though the FASTQ file is fine?

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the answer -->

Does its explanation make sense to you?
Unlike an agent, Ask mode won't test its own claims ---
but you can easily do that yourself.
Run the following lines in the terminal
(`$?` contains the exit status of the last command, and `set +o pipefail`
turns the setting off again):

```bash
set -o pipefail
zcat ../../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz | head -n 8
echo $?
set +o pipefail
```

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>What does the exit status tell you?</summary>

An exit status of `0` means success, and anything else means failure.
You should see `141`, which means that `zcat` was killed by a "`SIGPIPE`" signal
because `head` stopped reading after 8 lines.
With `pipefail`, that failure becomes the exit status of the whole pipeline,
and with `set -e`, the script would stop at this line.

</details>

Finally, ask a follow-up question:

> How can I avoid this?

Copilot will likely give you several options.
Which one would you choose, and why?

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Using code from an answer
When an answer includes a code block,
hover over it to see buttons to copy the code, insert it at the cursor,
or insert it into a new file.
:::

#### More example prompts for Ask mode

Here are some more questions that you could ask in Ask mode:

- What is the difference between `"$@"` and `$@` in a Bash script?
- What does a base quality score of 30 in a FASTQ file mean,
  and how is it encoded?
- Why are the reads of paired-end FASTQ files stored in two separate files,
  and how do the two files relate to each other?
- What is the difference between `git restore`, `git reset`, and `git revert`?
- What does `oras://` mean at the start of an Apptainer image URL?
- Why should I use a container image with an exact version,
  rather than the latest version?

### Some examples in "Agent" mode

Select "Agent" mode.
Your workspace is `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`,
which contains all of your work for this course,
so Copilot can find and use files from earlier weeks.

Let's start with this prompt:

> Write a shell script to run the program FastQC on one FASTQ file

![](/img/copilot-agent-fastqc.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot Agent mode finding the existing fastqc.sh script and proposing an example command to run it." .lightbox}

Just like Claude would, it first searched your workspace,
and found the `fastqc.sh` script that you wrote in week 7!
And look at the example usage, where it has found my dir with FASTQ files,
but ...

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>What mistake can you spot in the screenshot above?</summary>

There is no `sample1_R1.fastq` file in that dir ---
the Garrigos data files are named completely differently.

</details>

Let's ask for an edit to that script:

> Add code to print the date before and after running FastQC

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the edit with Keep/Undo -->

Unlike in Claude's "Manual" permission mode,
where Claude asks permission _before_ it edits a file,
Copilot makes the edits right away.
You then review the changes, which are shown as "diffs"
(remember this from Git?),
and either keep or undo them,
either all at once or bit-by-bit.

What about:

> Write a similar script but to run the program trimgalore

![](/img/copilot-agent-trimgalore2.png){fig-align="center" width="98%" fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot Agent mode creating a new TrimGalore script based on existing scripts it found in the project dir." .lightbox}

It found TrimGalore scripts elsewhere in the project dir
and created a new script based on those!
Again, you still need to "approve" the final creation of the file,
e.g. by clicking "Keep" in the chat window on the right,
or the checkmark icon in the top-right of the editor window
(see the screenshot above).

Finally, let's have the agent create a script to run a program for which we
don't have code yet ---
the program FeatureCounts, which can be used to count reads mapping to genes^[
This is similar to the program Salmon which was indicated in our workflow diagrams.]:

> Create a script to run the program FeatureCounts on BAM files in a given directory

![](/img/copilot-agent-featurecounts-full.png){fig-align="center" width="98%" fig-alt="A screenshot of Copilot Agent mode creating a new script to run FeatureCounts on BAM files." .lightbox}

::: {.callout-note}
#### Running commands
Just like Claude, Copilot asks for permission before it runs a command.
And just like with Claude, read every command before you approve it!
:::

### An example in "Plan" mode

Select "Plan" mode and type the following prompt:

> I want a runner script that first runs my FastQC script and then my TrimGalore
> script on all samples in ../../garrigos/fastq. Make a plan for this.

<!-- TODO: screenshot of the plan -->

Just like with Claude's Plan mode,
Copilot looks through your files but doesn't change anything.
Then, it shows a plan in the chat,
and may ask you some questions about choices it had to make.

Read the plan carefully:

- Does it use your existing scripts, rather than writing new ones?
- Does it correctly find the sample names,
  and pair the R1 and R2 files of each sample?

If not, reply with feedback, and Copilot will update the plan.
Once you're happy with it,
click the button to start the implementation:
this switches to Agent mode, which will carry out the plan.

## Appendix

### Copilot custom "background" instructions

Just like you can give Claude persistent instructions with a `CLAUDE.md` file,
you can provide custom instructions to GitHub Copilot that will guide
its behavior across all your questions.
For example, let's say you want to ask it to create a series of Bash scripts
one-after-another,
and all with some of the same settings and header comments that we've been using
(or some others that you prefer!).

Copilot doesn't read `CLAUDE.md`, but it does read an `AGENTS.md` file
in your project root, which many AI coding tools use.
Alternatively, you can use a Copilot-specific file:

1. Create a new folder called `.github` in your project root.
2. Inside the `.github` folder, create a file called `copilot-instructions.md`.
3. In that file, write your custom instructions in Markdown format.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
For more info, see
[these VS Code docs](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/getting-started#_create-custom-instructions)
:::

### Copilot advanced chat usage with "slash commands" and more

As the chat window shows in ghost text,
you can use keyboard shortcuts to activate certain options:

- Context (files) with `#` (in Claude, this is `@`):
  - `#file` to attach a relevant file

- "Slash commands" with `/`, just like in Claude
  (but the available commands differ):
  - `/explain` to get code explanations
  - `/fix` to receive a proposed fix for the problems in the selected code
  - `/simplify` to simplify the selected code

- Extensions with `@` (unlike in Claude, where `@` adds files):
  - e.g. `@workspace`

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-note
